items.body_md:
On September 2, plaintiffs Andrea Bartz, Andrea Bartz, Inc., Charles Graeber, Kirk Wallace Johnson, and MJ + KJ, Inc. filed a Status Report — Dkt. 688 — the first substantive filing from the plaintiff class since the July 20 final approval order. The specific contents of the status report are not yet available through RECAP/CourtListener, which reflects a last-updated timestamp of September 1 and has not ingested the September 2 and September 3 entries; the filing's subject matter and any positions taken are therefore unconfirmed and will require direct PACER access to assess. A status report at this stage — post-final-approval, with two fee appeals pending at the Ninth Circuit and the first $450 million installment due September 25 — is most likely keyed to one or more of those live issues: the payment timeline, the class distribution mechanics, or the posture of the objector/intervenor activity described below. Its classification turns on content not yet visible, so it is flagged here for immediate follow-up rather than characterized.

Also on September 3, Dkt. 690 — a Letter — appeared on the district docket. A letter to the court at this stage of a post-judgment, post-approval proceeding can range from ministerial to substantive depending on who sent it and what it requests; the docket entry supplies no party attribution or subject matter, and RECAP has not captured the document. It cannot be classified without the underlying text. Both Dkt. 688 and Dkt. 690 should be pulled directly from PACER before any inference is drawn about their bearing on recovery posture or the payment schedule. Separately, the September 2 docket also reflects an electronic filing error tied to objector Stacy Lynn Werner's Dkt. 687 — the notice of appeal/request to intervene filed August 31. The clerk's error notation directed Werner's counsel to refile using the correct Notice of Appeal form for the Ninth Circuit. That correction is procedural and carries no legal consequence for Werner's appeal on its merits; what matters is whether a conforming notice of appeal is subsequently filed and whether the Ninth Circuit opens a docket number for Werner's intervention effort alongside Nos. 26-5391 and 26-5455.

The two fee appeals — No. 26-5391 (Edelson PC / Oppenheim + Zebrak) and No. 26-5455 (Cowan DeBaets Abrahams & Sheppard LLP), both appealing the July 20 judgment's attorney's fees allocation — remain the substantive spine of the post-approval docket, as covered by __[Scrivener's Error](https://scrivenerserror.blogspot.com/)__ and confirmed by the district docket. Neither appeal affects Anthropic's payment obligations; no party has moved for a stay. The Ninth Circuit has not yet issued scheduling orders setting opening-brief deadlines in either appeal, an open question from prior briefings that remains unresolved. The next concrete milestone is Anthropic's $450 million Scheduled Payment 1, due September 25, 2026. The content of Dkt. 688 and Dkt. 690 — once accessible via PACER — is the most immediate priority for assessing whether anything filed this week bears on that deadline or the class distribution posture.

items.body_md:
Today, Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants filed a letter from Lowenstein Sandler's Michael A. Kaplan to Judge Owens (Dkt. 235) proposing a schedule for proceedings in connection with the pending motion to dismiss (Dkt. 93) — a filing that matters because it signals the opposing coalition is moving to shape the litigation calendar for the dismissal fight rather than waiting for the court to set it unilaterally. The letter is the first affirmative scheduling proposal from the Omnis Fuel / Quantum side regarding the dismissal motion, and its filing the morning of the final cash collateral and bidding procedures hearing suggests that side intends to press both tracks simultaneously. 
The dismissal motion is not before Judge Owens today and carries a hearing scheduled approximately 60 days out, but Judge Owens may approve, deny, modify, or defer some or all of the immediate relief requested today while that underlying challenge remains unresolved.
 A scheduling letter on the dismissal track, filed concurrently with an amended witness-and-exhibit list (Dkt. 234) for today's hearing, makes clear that Omnis Fuel / Quantum are litigating both fronts in parallel.

Also filed today, Judge Owens entered an order granting the prepetition secured parties leave to file their reply to objections to the bidding procedures motion and reserving rights on cash collateral (Dkt. 228, related to Dkts. 213 and 214). That order clears TRAG and RG Energy's reply for the record ahead of today's contested session. 
The debtor is seeking final authority to use cash collateral and provide protections to TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC, approval of bidding procedures for a sale of the operating plant, and approval of professionals proposed to conduct the bankruptcy and sale.
 
Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants filed four objections; WVEDA and the U.S. Trustee filed separate, independent objections.
 On the Lowenstein Sandler admission front, Judge Owens also signed PHV orders today for Lauren M. Laino (Dkt. 242) and Nicole M. Fulfree (Dkt. 241) — both of Lowenstein Sandler, filed on behalf of Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants (Dkts. 237, 236) — joining the Sidley Austin admissions for Kenneth W. Irvin and Jackson T. Garvey (Dkts. 239, 240) on the debtor's side. Dkts. 239–242 are procedural-and-routine, but the Lowenstein Sandler additions confirm that Omnis Fuel / Quantum are fielding a full trial team for today's hearing and beyond. The amended agenda (Dkt. 238) confirms the hearing is proceeding at 11:30 a.m. ET at the Wilmington courthouse, Courtroom 3.

The stakes at today's hearing are not symmetric across the creditor body. 
WVEDA, which holds a claim exceeding $50 million arising from a loan to Quantum Pleasants that Omnis Pleasants guaranteed, objects that portions of the proposed lender protections are "over-reaching," warns they could give TRAG and RG Energy a veto over the debtor's restructuring, and argues the proposed credit-bid treatment could chill third-party bidding.
 A final cash collateral order that locks in TRAG and RG Energy's adequate protection package on current terms would entrench their priority position ahead of any § 363 sale — compressing the pool available to WVEDA (which has not joined the dismissal motion) and to unsecured creditors. The Industrial Accessories mechanics lien (Dkt. 222, covering more than $4.4 million on a $10.7 million contract), perfected under § 546(b) and already in the record, will factor into that priority calculus as well. No post-hearing orders have appeared on the docket as of this writing; today's rulings — on cash collateral, bidding procedures, HSF Kramer's retention, and the AP Services / CEO application — are the next concrete milestone, with any resulting orders expected to be entered by Judge Owens in the near term following argument.

items.lede: Today, six documents — Dkts. 194 through 199 — appeared on the Poolin docket, five filed September 2 and one filed September 3, with no publicly indexed metadata identifying their content, filer, or title.
items.body_md:
Today, six documents — Dkts. 194 through 199 — appeared on the Poolin docket, five filed September 2 and one filed September 3, with no publicly indexed metadata identifying their content, filer, or title. None of the available secondary sources describe these filings, and CM/ECF and __[Verita Global](https://veritaglobal.net/poolin)__ are the only routes to confirm their classification. Until those pleadings are retrieved directly, classification is impossible: if any of the six constitutes a bid submission, a sale objection, a motion to adjourn the auction, or any supplemental filing tied to the Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190, it would be substantive and material. Any creditor tracking recovery exposure must pull them before tomorrow's close of business — the qualified bid deadline is September 8, five calendar days away.

The sale process is now in its final approach. 
The August 17 order set September 8 as the deadline for qualified bids, with an auction scheduled for September 10 if competing offers emerge.
 
The auction, if triggered, is to be held at 10:00 a.m. Eastern, either at the offices of Archer & Greiner in Voorhees, New Jersey, virtually, or at another time and place designated by the debtors.
 
Thor CALAP LLC has agreed to serve as stalking-horse bidder with a $52 million offer, allocating $37 million to the Tarbush power rights and equipment and $15 million to the Pyote property.
 That floor represents roughly 32 cents on the dollar against the $163.7 million IOU pool, before administrative and priority claims. 
AI infrastructure operators drove meaningful interest during marketing because of the sites' existing grid connections and electrical capacity
 — which is the strongest argument for a bid above the stalking-horse floor, but 28 NDAs, seven LOIs, and three additional indications of interest during marketing did not produce a disclosed competing bid before today. Whether any of Dkts. 194–199 changes that picture is the central unknown.

The Rule 9019 compromise at Dkt. 190 (filed August 28) remains unresolved: its counterparty, subject matter, and dollar amount are not disclosed in public metadata, and the objection deadline running approximately 21 days from filing ripens around September 18 — the same date as the 
sale hearing following the September 10 auction.
 Separately, 
the Bondoro case summary lists the sale hearing as September 16 and an outside closing date of November 30, 2026
 — the September 16 date conflicts with the September 18 date appearing in multiple other sources; creditors should confirm against the operative scheduling order on the docket. The October 21 trustee hearing remains the case's largest structural overhang: a creditor's motion alleging that the company's principal absconded from China to the U.S. with customer funds, if granted, would displace existing management and the CRO, transfer control of the § 363 sale and the 9019 settlement to a court-appointed fiduciary, and restructure who makes distributions to the 11,700 IOU holders. The next hard deadline is September 8.

items.lede: On September 2, Judge Walrath signed an order granting in part Skillz Platform Inc.'s motion to compel production of documents and a witness for deposition (Dkt. 92, resolving Dkts. 73, 78, and 91).
items.body_md:
On September 2, Judge Walrath signed an order granting in part Skillz Platform Inc.'s motion to compel production of documents and a witness for deposition (Dkt. 92, resolving Dkts. 73, 78, and 91). This is the most significant substantive development since the case was filed: the court has now directed discovery against the foreign representative in a Chapter 15 proceeding where the foreign representative has resisted production, and a partial grant means Judge Walrath credited Skillz's arguments on at least some of the disputed requests while limiting or denying others. The exact scope of what was compelled — which documents, which deponent, and on what timeline — is not disclosed on the face of the docket entry; the order itself controls, and reading the granular holdings will determine whether Skillz obtained what it needs to build a factual record on the recognition contest or was cut back to something narrower.

The path to Dkt. 92 is straightforward from the prior docket. Skillz filed its motion to compel (Dkt. 73), the foreign representative opposed (Dkt. 78) and supplemented (Dkt. 81), Skillz filed certified English translations of underlying foreign-proceeding documents (Dkt. 84), and the August 28 hearing produced a minute entry directing an order under certification of counsel (Dkt. 85). Skillz filed that certification on September 1 (Dkt. 91), and the order followed the next morning. Dkt. 90, filed September 1, is a notice of service of Oriel Bachar's responses and objections to Skillz's first set of interrogatories — substantive-but-routine at this stage, confirming the foreign representative served written responses to Skillz's interrogatories, though the content of those objections may become a flashpoint if Skillz views them as deficient relative to the newly-issued compel order.

For recovery posture, the partial grant cuts both ways. Skillz has now secured court-ordered access to at least some of the financial and operational information it needs to contest recognition or to argue that the Israeli proceeding does not qualify as a foreign main proceeding — or, failing that, to attack the adequacy of the debt settlement plan that Judge Lushi-Abudi in Tel Aviv has already told Papaya must be strengthened beyond operating-profit reliance, per the __[Firy/FIRY press release carried by StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/FIRY/israeli-court-says-papaya-gaming-should-improve-its-debt-settlement-81are4y0jeia.html)__ dated August 26. The "in part" qualifier matters for Papaya: it signals that Judge Walrath drew some limit on the scope of Skillz's discovery demands, preserving at least a partial objection from the foreign representative. The next concrete milestones are compliance with Dkt. 92's production and deposition directives (deadlines to be confirmed from the order itself) and the setting of a recognition hearing date, which has not yet appeared on the docket.

items.lede: On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here.
items.body_md:
On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here. Given the live motions practice in this case, the most plausible target is Google's August 21 Administrative Motion to Consider Whether Cases Should Be Related (Dkt. 478), whose response deadline was set at August 25 — the same date Dkt. 483 was filed. If that is the motion being opposed, the filing reflects a party — most likely the plaintiff class — resisting Google's effort to link this proceeding to one or more related cases. The case-relation motion, if granted, could shift judicial assignment or coordinate discovery and briefing schedules in ways that affect litigation pace and cost for both sides; if denied, each proceeding continues on its own track. Until Dkt. 483's full text is pulled from PACER, the identity of the filing party, the motion it targets, and the arguments advanced remain unverified and are not stated here.

The more consequential open question from yesterday remains unresolved in any available source: the outcome of the Dkt. 482 omnibus order — which adjudicates class certification, Google's sanctions motion, the outstanding intervention motion (Dkt. 468, Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix), and three motions for miscellaneous relief — has not been reported by any secondary outlet as of this briefing. The full text of Dkt. 482 on PACER is the controlling document. Until it is pulled, the class's shape, the sanctions disposition, and whether the intervenors were admitted remain unverified. The practical consequence is significant: class certification in this case defines the universe of copyright holders who can share in any statutory-damages recovery, and the per-work structure of § 504(c) means that the breadth of the certified class — authors only, publishers included, works defined by training vs. ingestion — directly sets the ceiling on Google's aggregate exposure.

The next concrete milestone is the resolution of the Dkt. 478 case-relation motion, which is now fully briefed with Dkt. 483's opposition and ripe for ruling. No hearing date is visible in the docket text for that motion. On the merits track, the full text of Dkt. 482 — available on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 — remains the priority pull; it is the document that determines where this case goes from here.

items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
